summary.text: The Keeling Curve is a graph of carbon dioxide in Earth's air, built from continuous readings at Hawaii's Mauna Loa Observatory from 1958 to today.
Its steady climb gave the first significant evidence that CO₂ levels were rising rapidly, a rise caused by burning fossil fuels.
A yearly wiggle of about 6 ppm tracks Northern Hemisphere plants drawing CO₂ out of the air in spring and summer, then releasing it as they decay.

items.prompt: Each year the CO₂ reading at Mauna Loa peaks around May and falls until September. What mostly drives that drop?

options.label: The volcano releases less gas in summer
Northern plants growing and taking up CO₂
Warm oceans pulling extra gas out of the air
People burning less fuel in warm months

items.explain: Most land vegetation is in the Northern Hemisphere, and its spring and summer growth removes CO₂ through photosynthesis until the September low.

items.prompt: You want CO₂ readings that reflect the wider atmosphere rather than one patch of countryside. Which kind of site best fits that goal?

options.label: A dense forest where plants trade lots of gas
The edge of a big city full of traffic
A spot far from continents with bare ground
A sheltered valley where the air sits still

items.explain: Mauna Loa was picked because it is remote, far from continents, and has little vegetation to skew the readings.

items.prompt: In 1938 Guy Callendar compared old CO₂ readings and concluded that human emissions were raising them. Why did most scientists not accept this?

options.label: His readings were scattered and irregular
Everyone already knew CO₂ was falling
He blamed volcanoes instead of people
His numbers showed no change over time

items.explain: Callendar's conclusion was widely rejected because the measurements behind it were patchy.

items.prompt: Testing his instruments in forests, Keeling found more CO₂ at night than in the afternoon. What explains the night-time excess?

options.label: Cool night air dissolves extra gas from dew
Traffic and heating peak after dark
The sensors drift when there is no light
Plants and soils keep respiring at night

items.explain: Respiration by plants and soils adds CO₂ at night, while afternoon values better reflect the wider air.

items.prompt: Over the decades the curve has kept climbing, and the climb has sped up recently. What is causing the long-term rise?

options.label: Gas leaking from Mauna Loa's own vents
More plants decaying every autumn
The burning of fossil fuels
A slow natural rise in sunlight

items.explain: The rise in atmospheric CO₂ comes from fossil fuel combustion and has been accelerating in recent years.

items.prompt: Mauna Loa readings started in March 1958. By November 2018, roughly how much had average CO₂ climbed?

options.label: About 10 ppm
About 300 ppm
About 1,000 ppm
About 90 ppm

items.explain: The average rose from 313 ppm to 406 ppm, a climb of about 93 ppm.
